newsitem.title: UK: Shipowners concerned at lack of pollution cover.
newsitem.headline: Shipowners concerned at lack of pollution cover.

text.p: Tanker owners are concerned at the lack of pollution cover for oil spills off countries not ratifying international civil liability and fund conventions following the ending of a voluntary agreement, according to an owners federation.

The Tanker Owners Voluntary Agreement concerning Liability for Oil Pollution (Tovalop) was terminated as of February 20. But the International Tanker Owners Pollution Federation (ITOPF), which had administered the scheme, said it was receiving queries from tanker owners regarding the situation with countries not ratifying international conventions intended to replace Tovalop.
ITOPF technical manager Joe Nichols said: "Those countries not ratifying the convention may have a problem."
He added that it was unclear what would happen in the event of an oil spill off a country not covered by international pollution compensation conventions.

Most major maritime states have ratified the International Convention on Civil Liability for Oil Pollution Damage (CLC) or the International Convention on the Establishment of an International Fund for Compensation for Oil Pollution Damage (Fund Convention) and the CLC.
But there are several countries with vulnerable coasts which have no arrangements - including Turkey, Argentina, Uruguay, Iran and Thailand.

Uruguay has narrowly missed becoming a test case for the new situation in the wake of a spill reported of at least 200 tonnes from a Panamanian flag tanker which grounded off its coast on February 8. Oil from the 67,031dwt San Jorge was washed ashore on beaches close to the resort of Punta del Este.
Observers believe that countries without convention cover could resort to arresting ships in order to recover pollution damages.
P&I insurers could apply the laws of the land where spills occur, but these might not provide much cover.
However, Nichols said: "The hope is that countries which have not ratified are alert to the problems and are taking urgent steps to ratify the conventions."

Meanwhile, ITOPF is recommending that its members display notices onboard explaining why Tovalop certificates are no longer being carried as there may still be some port authorities and terminal operators requesting the documentation.
ITOPF also pointed out that tankers will still carry their own pollution insurance.

The CLC, which entered force in 1975, lays down the principle of strict liability for shipowners and creates a system of compulsory liability insurance which is normally limited to the tonnage of a ship.
The Fund Convention, which is supplementary to the CLC, establishes a regime for compensating pollution victims when the CLC is inadequate. It entered force in 1978.
Around 97 percent of the world's tanker tonnage was entered under the Tovalop agreement which mirrored the the provisions of the international pollution conventions.
The US is also not a party to either convention because it relies on its own Oil Pollution Act of 1990 which imposes stringent liability provisions.
